title: Secure Design Principles
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 3: Security Architecture and Engineering: Secure Design Principles.

blocks.text: Defense in Depth

items: Apply multiple layers of security controls (layered defense)
No single control should be the sole protection for any asset
Layers should include administrative, technical, and physical controls
Also called layered security or onion defense
If one layer fails, others continue to provide protection

blocks.text: 📚 Extended Notes
Defense in depth ensures that an attacker must bypass multiple security controls to reach an asset. Example layers for a data center:

items: Perimeter — Fences, gates, guards
Building — Locks, badge readers, CCTV
Server room — Biometric access, mantrap
Network — Firewalls, IDS/IPS, segmentation
Host — OS hardening, antimalware, patching
Application — Input validation, authentication
Data — Encryption, access controls, DLP

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: "Defense in depth" is listed as an example of secure design principles alongside threat modeling, least privilege, and secure defaults. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Defense in depth is not just about having multiple firewalls (that's defense in breadth). True defense in depth uses DIFFERENT types of controls at DIFFERENT layers.
Zero Trust Architecture

items: Never trust, always verify — replaces "trust but verify"
Assume the network is always hostile, even internal
Verify every access request regardless of source location
Micro-segmentation limits lateral movement
Implemented through Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)

blocks.text: 📚 Extended Notes
From Destination CISSP, the seven tenets of Zero Trust:

items: Know your architecture (users, devices, and services)
Know your user, service, and device identities
Know the health of your users, devices, and services
Use policies to authorize requests
Authenticate everywhere
Focus your monitoring on devices and services
Don't trust any network

blocks.text: From Stewart: "Due to the rapid growth and changes in the modern threatscape, the trust but verify model of security is no longer sufficient. Most security experts now recommend designing organizational security around the zero-trust model." Zero trust is particularly relevant in modern environments with:

items: Remote workers accessing resources from anywhere
Cloud services spanning multiple providers
BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) policies
IoT devices with limited security capabilities

blocks.text: Least Privilege and Need to Know

items: Users receive minimum access required for their job function
Need to know adds context — access based on legitimate business requirement
Applies to users, processes, and systems
Reduces attack surface and limits damage from compromise
Must be reviewed regularly to prevent privilege creep

blocks.text: 📚 Extended Notes
Least privilege and need to know work together:

items: Least privilege defines the minimum LEVEL of access
Need to know defines WHETHER access is needed at all

blocks.text: Example: A system administrator may have the technical privilege to access all databases (least privilege for their role), but they should only access databases relevant to their current work assignment (need to know). Privilege creep occurs when users accumulate access rights over time as they change roles or take on new responsibilities without having old access revoked.
Secure Defaults and Fail-Secure

items: Systems should default to the most secure configuration
Fail-secure (fail-closed) — System denies access on failure (e.g., locked door on power loss)
Fail-open — System allows access on failure (used for life safety, e.g., fire exit)
Default-deny is preferred over default-allow
All unnecessary features/ports/services should be disabled by default

blocks.text: 📚 Extended Notes
From Stewart: Secure design includes "managing secure defaults, designing a system to fail securely." Fail-secure vs. Fail-open:

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Life safety ALWAYS takes priority over security. If a fire occurs, doors must fail-open even if that means security is temporarily compromised.
Separation of Duties and Mechanisms

items: Separation of mechanisms — Security mechanisms should be independent
Compromise of one mechanism should not compromise others
Critical processes require multiple approvals (two-person control)
System administration and security audit should be separate roles
Supports defense in depth by ensuring independent control layers

blocks.text: Keep It Simple

items: Also called Economy of Mechanism
Simpler systems have fewer vulnerabilities
Complex systems are harder to secure, test, and audit
Minimize the attack surface by reducing unnecessary features
Prefer proven, simple solutions over complex ones

blocks.text: 📚 Extended Notes
From Destination CISSP: In the context of designing and building a secure system, simplicity results in:

items: Smaller attack surface
Fewer errors and vulnerabilities
Less complex testing

blocks.text: The "KISS" principle (Keep It Simple, Stupid) applies directly to security architecture. Every additional feature, service, or interface is a potential attack vector.
Privacy by Design

items: Integrate privacy protections into system design from the beginning
Not an afterthought — build privacy into the architecture
Seven foundational principles (developed by Ann Cavoukian)
Required by GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design)
Includes data minimization, purpose limitation, and transparency
